# build


<!-- WARNING: THIS FILE WAS AUTOGENERATED! DO NOT EDIT! -->

This module runs a build. A Mac build has requirements that are easy to
get wrong: py2app needs a framework build of Python, the bundle should
contain the exact package versions in `uv.lock`, and a build must not
overwrite an app that is running. Afterwards you want to know which
commit an app came from.
[`check`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#check)
reports on all of this without changing anything, and
[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build) does
the work.

### run

``` python
def run(
    *args, **kw
):
```

[`run`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#run) prints a
command, prefixed with `·`, and runs it, raising an error if the command
fails. Every external command a build runs goes through it, so the build
log shows each one.

``` python
run('echo', 'built')
```

    · echo built

    CompletedProcess(args=['echo', 'built'], returncode=0)

### lock_requirements

``` python
def lock_requirements(
    root, extras:tuple=(), out:NoneType=None
):
```

*Export the `uv.lock` in `root` as a pinned requirements file and return
its path, or `None` if that is not possible.*

A bundle should contain the package versions your project was tested
with.
[`lock_requirements`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#lock_requirements)
asks uv to export the `uv.lock` in `root` as a pinned requirements file,
including the optional dependency groups named in `extras`, and writes
it to `out`, by default `packaging/.app-venv/app-requirements.txt`. It
returns the file’s path, or `None` when there is no `uv.lock` or the
export fails.
[`build_venv`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build_venv)
takes `None` to mean that it should install from `pyproject.toml`
instead, with whatever versions pip picks.

``` python
tmp = TemporaryDirectory(); root = Path(tmp.name)
lock_requirements(root) is None
```

    True

### build_venv

``` python
def build_venv(
    python, venv, root, extras:tuple=(), force:bool=False
):
```

*Create or update the build venv at `venv` from `python`, install the
project with pinned requirements, and return its Python.*

[`build_venv`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build_venv)
prepares the environment a macOS build runs in. It creates a virtual
environment at `venv` from the interpreter `python`, starting again if
`force` is set or if the existing one was made with a different Python
version. It installs the pinned requirements from
[`lock_requirements`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#lock_requirements)
when there are any, installs the project at `root` in editable mode with
its `extras`, and returns the path of the environment’s Python.
[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build) calls
it. It has no example here because it installs packages.

### git_stamp

``` python
def git_stamp(
    root, version:str=''
):
```

*Return the commit, dirty flag, version and build time for the checkout
at `root`, or `None` outside one.*

A bundle is a copy of your code, and nothing in it says which version of
the source it came from. A stamp records that. It is a small JSON file
named `build.json` (the name is in `STAMP`) that holds the git commit,
whether the checkout had uncommitted changes, the version and the build
time.

[`stamp_path`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#stamp_path)
says where the stamp goes: inside `Contents/Resources` for a `.app`, and
next to the executable for anything else. It decides by the `.app`
suffix alone, so it works for a bundle that has not been built yet.

``` python
stamp_path('/dist/Demo.app'), stamp_path('/dist/Demo')
```

    (Path('/dist/Demo.app/Contents/Resources/build.json'),
     Path('/dist/Demo/build.json'))

[`git_stamp`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#git_stamp)
collects the stamp’s fields from the git checkout at `root`, or returns
`None` if `root` is not in one.
[`write_stamp`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#write_stamp)
writes the stamp into a bundle and returns it. Outside a checkout the
commit is left empty, and if the bundle’s folder does not exist nothing
is written.
[`read_stamp`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#read_stamp)
reads the stamp back, and returns `None` if the bundle has none or it
cannot be parsed.

``` python
st = write_stamp(repo/'dist'/'Demo.app', repo, version='2.0.1')
st['commit'][:12], st['dirty'], st['version']
```

    ('3b2bbb3a952a', False, '2.0.1')

``` python
read_stamp(repo/'dist'/'Demo.app') == st
```

    True

If tracked files have changes that are not committed, the stamp says
`dirty`, and
[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build) prints
that next to the commit. When an app misbehaves, you can then tell
whether it was built from code that was never committed.

``` python
(repo/'x.txt').write_text('changed')
git_stamp(repo)['dirty']
```

    True

### check

``` python
def check(
    spec, root, venv:NoneType=None
):
```

*Report what a build would do on this machine without doing it; works on
any platform, Linux included.*

[`check`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#check)
reports what
[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build) would
do on this machine, as a dict, without building anything or changing any
files. It names the platform, the interpreter and the freezer, says
whether pywebview is installed, and lists the process IDs of any running
copies of the app. On macOS it also says whether the current Python is a
framework build and, if it is not, which framework Python and which
build environment
[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build) would
use instead. On Linux it says that nothing can be built there: a Mac app
is built on macOS and a Windows app on Windows. Run it first when a
build fails before it starts. The example replaces two machine-specific
paths in the result.

``` python
demo = App(name='Demo', entry='demo_app.py', version='2.0.1')
rep = check(demo, repo)
{**rep, 'interpreter': '/proj/.venv/bin/python3', 'out': '/proj/dist/Demo'}
```

    {'platform': 'linux',
     'interpreter': '/proj/.venv/bin/python3',
     'app': 'Demo',
     'out': '/proj/dist/Demo',
     'freezer': 'none — linux builds nothing; macOS and Windows build on their own OS',
     'pywebview': 'MISSING',
     'running': []}

### build

``` python
def build(
    spec, root, setup_py, venv:NoneType=None, alias:bool=False, force:bool=False, rebuild_venv:bool=False,
    identity:NoneType=None
):
```

*Freeze `spec` into `root/dist`, switching to a framework Python first
on macOS when needed.*

[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build)
freezes `spec` into `root/dist` and returns the path of the result.
`setup_py` is the script that calls the freezer for your app. It will
not start while a copy of the app is running, unless you pass
`force=True`, because the build replaces the standard library the
running app imports from, and that app then fails with a zip error that
says nothing about the build.

On macOS it next checks the interpreter. If the current Python is not a
framework build,
[`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build) finds
one with
[`framework_python`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/probe.html#framework_python),
prepares an environment with
[`build_venv`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build_venv)
(pass `rebuild_venv=True` to make it from scratch), runs the script that
called [`build`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/build.html#build)
again with that environment’s Python, and returns. The environment
variable `KAVACHA_BUILD_VENV` (the name is in `REEXEC`) marks the second
run, so a Python that is still unsuitable stops the build instead of
looping.

On a framework Python, and on Windows, it runs the freezer, calls
[`finish`](https://vedicreader.github.io/kavacha/bundle.html#finish) on
macOS with `identity`, writes the stamp, and prints where the app is and
which commit it was built from. `alias=True` asks py2app for an alias
build, which refers to your source files instead of copying them and is
quicker while you develop.
